question: The assembler's finished work lives in two places: this machine, and the shared copy the other tools read from. Only the shared copy is visible to anyone else. Back in August a run of eighty finished pieces sat on this machine alone for weeks, and you approved sending them up once. That approval covered that one time. I need to know whether sending finished work up is something I just do from now on, or something I ask about each time.

options.name: Send finished work up whenever it is ready
options.what: Anything I finish becomes visible to the other tools the same day. Nothing is ever overwritten or rewritten; work is only ever added on top of what is already there.
options.costs: You lose a look at the work before it becomes visible to the rest of the suite. In practice that look has never caught anything, because the other tools cannot use the work until it is up there anyway.

options.name: Ask you every time
options.what: Nothing becomes visible to the other tools until you say so.
options.costs: Roughly one interruption per finished piece, and any other tool waiting to point at that work waits for you. That is exactly how the eighty piece backlog happened.

recommend.because: The other tools cannot reference our work at all until it is up there, so holding it back does not protect anything, it just delays them. It only ever adds, never replaces, so there is nothing to undo if you dislike something. If you would rather see specific kinds of work first, name the kind and I will hold just those.

question: Forty eight days ago you said the inner workings of the assembler were out of your wheelhouse and told me to make the best decisions and get on with it. Every session since has run on that, and nobody has checked with you once in all that time. It is doing real work, so I am not asking you to withdraw it. I am asking how much you want to hear about what gets decided under it.

options.name: Keep it as it is, and hear about it at milestones
options.what: I keep deciding, and you get told when a whole piece of work finishes rather than when each call inside it gets made.
options.costs: You will occasionally find out about a design choice after it is already built into everything. Unwinding one at that point is a day or two rather than a conversation.

options.name: Keep it, but tell you the notable calls as they happen
options.what: Same authority, but the handful of choices per piece of work that a person could reasonably disagree with get written down for you as they are made.
options.costs: A few short notes per piece of work landing on your screen. You can ignore them and lose nothing, but they are still there to read.

options.name: Take it back and decide these yourself
options.what: Internal choices come to you before they are built.
options.costs: Several decisions a day, most of them about things you told me you had no interest in. Work stops between each one.

recommend.because: Keeping the authority is clearly right, since it has produced a working assembler without you having to think about any of it. The only thing worth changing is that right now nothing is written down for you at all, so the first you hear of a choice is when something built on it goes wrong. A short note per notable call costs me nothing and gives you a place to object early.

question: The tool I look after is two things at once. It is a machine that turns the game's source into a cartridge, and it is also the language that source is written in. You told me the machine half is mine to decide. The language half is different: adding a new word to it changes what every future page of game source looks like, and it is close to impossible to take one back once the game is written using it. I have been treating any new word as yours and everything else as mine, and I want to know if that is where you want the line drawn. This is the one of my three questions that is actually holding work up.

options.name: Any new word in the language comes to you
options.what: I decide how the machine works and how anything already in the language is spelled. Anything genuinely new waits for you.
options.costs: Two warnings the build has been printing since the eighteenth of August cannot be cleared, because clearing them needs a new way of writing one kind of import. They will keep printing until you rule. Every future addition waits on you the same way.

options.name: New words are mine unless they change what ends up on the cartridge
options.what: I can add ways of writing things that produce exactly the same cartridge bytes as today. Anything that changes what actually gets written into the cartridge still comes to you.
options.costs: The language grows without your sign off. The risk is a word you would not have chosen becoming normal across the game source before you see it. It is bounded by the fact that none of it can change the game as it runs.

options.name: The language is mine too, and you see it at milestones
options.what: I decide the whole thing and report at the end of each piece of work.
options.costs: You would be finding out about the shape of the language the game is written in after it is already written that way. This is the hardest one to reverse.

recommend.because: It splits on the thing that actually matters to you. A new way of writing something that produces an identical cartridge is a matter of taste in the source, and you have already said the source machinery is mine. A construct that changes what the cartridge contains is a real design decision about the game and should be yours. It clears the two stuck warnings immediately, and the padding construct that is genuinely a design call stays with you, which is where I think you want it.

detail: Concretely: the closure-edge import spelling that kills the two CORPUS_OPEN_FINDINGS rows (import.no-names, first_observed 2026-08-18, in crates/sigil-cli/tests/warn_tier_corpus.rs) is byte-neutral by construction and would fall to me under emit_line. pad_to(N) moves bytes the author did not write and stays with the owner under either as_now or emit_line. question: Content growth (a level, an object, a background band) currently bricks the build because the assembler places sections against a frozen table of addresses, and the tool that would refresh that table runs the same placement that just failed. You said get away from this now. Which shape do you want?

options.name: Refresh the frozen table once, with a real band present
options.what: I regenerate the table from a build that has one background band in it, and the frozen mechanism stays. The band builds today.
options.costs: The next time any section grows past its slot, the build bricks again and someone repeats this by hand. It fits exactly one band geometry; the next scene aurora authors can break it.

options.name: Derive placement from order and size; keep the table as an after-the-fact check (Recommended)
options.what: The build places sections from the map's declared order and their real sizes. The hardware-fixed addresses (DAC banks at 0x0/0x10000/0x48000, the bank bases) stay fixed; everything else floats. The frozen table becomes an expectation the test suite checks against, and a moved boundary prints a warning naming the section and the delta instead of failing the build. The engine lane keeps its byte-attribution tooling. First step is small (one file), byte-neutral while nothing has grown, and lets one band build without moving anything by hand.
options.costs: A couple of days across my lane and the engine lane: my parcel, then one refreeze through the engine lane. The engine's ceiling-printing script must be re-pointed. Sections that grow now move their neighbours silently-but-loudly (a warning, not a failure), so a byte-change you did not expect shows up as a warning line rather than a red build — you have to read the warning.

options.name: Delete the frozen tables outright
options.what: Same derived placement, but no committed table at all; the only frozen thing left is the ROM checksum where a shape is meant to be identical.
options.costs: The test suite loses the oracle that tells you WHICH section moved when a checksum changes; you find out by diffing. It also re-opens a code-size relaxation edge the tables currently guard. Buys nothing the checksum chain does not already prove.

recommend.because: The code is already most of the way there — order is map-driven and non-anchored sections already pack — so this removes the last three places the table decides bytes rather than redesigning placement. It is the only option that both builds today's band AND stops the next one from bricking the build, while keeping the loud-not-silent property the engine lane asked for. One warning to read beats a red build nobody can regenerate.

question: A struct in the game's source often ends with a filler field whose size someone worked out by hand. When a field above it changes, that number is silently wrong. I have drafted a way to let the author say where the next field should start and have the compiler work the filler out. Do you want it, and in which shape?

options.name: Both forms, plus a nudge when the risky one is used (Recommended)
options.what: Two ways to write filler: say where the next field starts and the compiler sizes it (the safe one), or say how many spare bytes you are reserving (the honest use of the second one — reserved space, where the count is the real intention). When someone writes the second in a place where the first was clearly meant, the build says so and prints the exact line to write instead.
options.costs: Two things to learn instead of one, and a new warning that could be wrong occasionally. The engine lane asked for only the first form and would be half-overruled here.

options.name: Only the safe form
options.what: One way to write filler: say where the next field starts. Nothing else is added to the language.
options.costs: Reserving a block of spare bytes — where the count IS the thing you mean, and the offset is what moves — has to be written by naming an offset you did not care about. The language already uses the other word elsewhere for exactly this, so refusing it here means the same word means different things in two places.

options.name: Not now
options.what: Leave it. The alignment check I shipped last week still catches a stale filler loudly; someone just has to fix the number by hand each time.
options.costs: The engine lane keeps hand-counting, and the one live case stays wrong-by-name (the field is called after the offset 93 and actually sits at 118).

recommend.because: The safe form is what the engine lane needs and it is in every option. The disagreement is only about whether to also keep the plain 'reserve N bytes' spelling: refusing it does not remove the hazard, because someone reserving spare bytes then has to write an offset they do not mean, and the word already means exactly that elsewhere in the language. A warning that names the mistake and prints the fix does more than removing the word would.

detail: PAD / queue item 4 (`pad_to(N)`). Draft committed at sigil docs/superpowers/notes/2026-08-26-pad-to-spec-draft.md (branch docs/pad-to-spec, 44d674a3), read against sigil 67dc3aef, empyrean origin/main 4a575c0, aeon origin/master bc95e32e. Grammar: anonymous markers `pad(expr)` / `pad_to(expr)` in a struct body, contextual keyword (ident + peek LParen), parseability confirmed against parser.rs::struct_decl, no collision with the by-name refusal of `@align(N)` or the trailing `(align:)` attribute. N = the offset the NEXT field starts at (a final pad's target is therefore the struct's total size). Zero width legal and inert; negative is `[layout.pad-overflow]` naming the field and both offsets with a byte delta, and explicitly telling the author NOT to convert it to a hand-counted width. Aeon's ask to drop struct-level `pad(N)` half-declined and argued in §1.5; their outcome delivered instead by a default-on `[layout.pad-hand-counted]` lint on the detectable shape (a `pad(N)` immediately followed by an `(align: N)` field) with a fix-it naming the exact `pad_to(N)`. `(align: N)` stays MANDATORY alongside (the silence argument: derivation must not absorb a defect the assertion detects); the ruling's falsifier is restated in the draft. Spec 2 §4.3's 'the compiler never inserts padding' survives verbatim and needs EXPLAINING, not amending. Six further open questions (Q1-Q7) are in the draft for later. Landing flag for empyrean: their spec at 4a575c0 does not document the `(align: N)` struct-field form at all, so both texts must land in one pass. Sigil does not land language spec: this goes to empyrean after you agree.

detail: PAD / queue item 4 (`pad_to(N)`). Draft committed at sigil docs/superpowers/notes/2026-08-26-pad-to-spec-draft.md (branch docs/pad-to-spec, 44d674a3), read against sigil 67dc3aef, empyrean origin/main 4a575c0, aeon origin/master bc95e32e. Grammar: anonymous markers `pad(expr)` / `pad_to(expr)` in a struct body, contextual keyword (ident + peek LParen), parseability confirmed against parser.rs::struct_decl, no collision with the by-name refusal of `@align(N)` or the trailing `(align:)` attribute. N = the offset the NEXT field starts at (a final pad's target is therefore the struct's total size). Zero width legal and inert; negative is `[layout.pad-overflow]` naming the field and both offsets with a byte delta, and explicitly telling the author NOT to convert it to a hand-counted width. Aeon's ask to drop struct-level `pad(N)` half-declined and argued in §1.5; their outcome delivered instead by a default-on `[layout.pad-hand-counted]` lint on the detectable shape (a `pad(N)` immediately followed by an `(align: N)` field) with a fix-it naming the exact `pad_to(N)`. `(align: N)` stays MANDATORY alongside (the silence argument: derivation must not absorb a defect the assertion detects); the ruling's falsifier is restated in the draft. Spec 2 §4.3's 'the compiler never inserts padding' survives verbatim and needs EXPLAINING, not amending. Six further open questions (Q1-Q7) are in the draft for later. Landing flag for empyrean: their spec at 4a575c0 does not document the `(align: N)` struct-field form at all, so both texts must land in one pass. They also named the two arguments they would not have reached: one word must not mean two things across two bodies, and prose discouragement IS a warning baseline — the same mechanism that let `[layout.odd-field]` drift for four commits. Their offer, accepted: they migrate `sc_pad_5D` the day it ships and report whether the fix-it's printed `pad_to(N)` was directly pasteable, which is the cheapest field test of the diagnostic text, after which their fixtures assert the exact strings as the cross-repo interface. So no lane now disputes the recommendation.

question: A struct in the game's source often ends with a filler field whose size someone worked out by hand. When a field above it changes, that number is silently wrong. I have drafted a way to let the author say where the next field should start and have the compiler work the filler out. Do you want it, and in which shape?

options.name: Both forms, plus a nudge when the risky one is used (Recommended)
options.what: Two ways to write filler: say where the next field starts and the compiler sizes it (the safe one), or say how many spare bytes you are reserving (the honest use of the second one — reserved space, where the count is the real intention). When someone writes the second in a place where the first was clearly meant, the build says so and prints the exact line to write instead.
options.costs: Two things to learn instead of one, and a new warning that could be wrong occasionally. The engine lane asked for only the first form and would be half-overruled here.

options.name: Only the safe form (the lane that asked for this has since withdrawn it)
options.what: One way to write filler: say where the next field starts. Nothing else is added to the language.
options.costs: Reserving a block of spare bytes — where the count IS the thing you mean, and the offset is what moves — has to be written by naming an offset you did not care about. The language already uses the other word elsewhere for exactly this, so refusing it here means the same word means different things in two places. The engine lane asked for this and has now read the argument and withdrawn it in their own words: they had generalised from their one case, and for reserving spare bytes the hazard inverts — the author would have to maintain a number that has nothing to do with what they meant, and every insertion above would turn a correct line into a build failure.

options.name: Not now
options.what: Leave it. The alignment check I shipped last week still catches a stale filler loudly; someone just has to fix the number by hand each time.
options.costs: The engine lane keeps hand-counting, and the one live case stays wrong-by-name (the field is called after the offset 93 and actually sits at 118).

recommend.because: Unchanged, and now uncontested: the lane that asked for the narrower option has read the argument and withdrawn it. The safe form is in every option; the only question was whether to also keep the plain 'reserve N bytes' spelling, and refusing it would make an author reserving spare bytes write an offset they do not mean, while the word already means exactly that elsewhere in the language. The warning that names the mistake and prints the fix does more than removing the word would.

detail: ANSWERED by the owner 2026-08-26, direct in this lane's session: 'yes' against the recommendation, so option 'both' is the ruling. Both spellings ship: pad_to(N) derives the filler width from the next field's offset, and the plain reserve-N-bytes form stays for the case where the count is the author's real intention, with a warning that names the mistake and prints the exact line to write when the deriving form was clearly meant. Read narrowly, 'yes' answers the 'do you want it' half outright and takes the recommended shape for the 'which shape' half; no separate option was named. Unblocks queue item PAD here and PAD-LAND at the hub, whose (b) leg lifts the spec text verbatim from docs/superpowers/notes/2026-08-26-pad-to-spec-draft.md at f49e56fc.

question: When engine source embeds a data file, the path is read from the project root - except one file, which writes its path relative to itself and works only because a single line in my tool names that file specifically. Do we keep relative-to-the-file as a real feature, or delete the exception and make the rule uniform?

options.what: The one file is respelled to use the project root like every other, and the special-case line is deleted. One rule, no exceptions, and it can finally be written down in the language spec.
options.costs: Two lines change in the engine source and three are deleted in my tool. The output is expected to be byte-for-byte identical, since the same file's contents are embedded either way - and that will be verified, not assumed. Nothing else in the tree uses the relative style.

options.what: Relative-to-the-file becomes a genuine, supported way to write these paths, available everywhere rather than to one named file.
options.costs: Real implementation work in the compiler, a new rule authors must learn, and two ways to spell the same thing forever. Buys convenience for files that sit deep in a directory tree.

options.what: Change nothing.
options.costs: The current state teaches every reader that relative paths work, when they work for exactly one hardcoded filename. The next person to copy that style gets a build failure and no clue why - and the line looks like a considered exception rather than the leftover it is.

recommend.because: This was never a decision anyone made. Measured in the engine's history and verified here with a positive control on the search: that file's relative spelling dates from 2026-07-09 and was among the first embeds in the tree; the earliest root-relative one is 2026-08-01, three weeks later, and 118 or so sites settled that way afterwards. So the odd one out is not a special need - it predates the convention it now violates, and the line naming it is a compatibility shim that has been quietly teaching everyone since that a feature exists which does not. Removing it costs a handful of lines and no bytes.

detail: Language surface, so his call rather than this lane's. Mechanism found by trace and confirmed by counterfactual (native.rs::build_emp's embed_base_for: `if id == "engine.math"`); note at sigil 6943cde3. Dates verified in aeon history with a positive control after the first two greps returned empty in a way a broken pattern would also produce. Byte-neutral either way; nothing is blocked on the answer.
